lessons.title: Intake procedures
lessons.html:
The receiving point

Fruit arrives at the packhouse in bins or crates on trucks and tractor-trailers from the orchards. The receiving or intake point is where the packhouse takes responsibility for the fruit. Good intake records are the start of traceability: every carton packed later must be linked back to the bins received here.

Information to capture

  • Date and time of arrival.
  • Producer (farm) and the orchard or block code.
  • Fruit kind and cultivar.
  • Number of bins or crates, and their numbers or tags if used.
  • Gross and nett mass if the fruit is weighed.
  • Picking date and, where applicable, the spray record or harvest clearance confirming withholding periods were respected.
  • Vehicle registration and driver's name.

Each delivery gets a delivery note or intake number. Bins are tagged or labelled so the batch stays identified through the whole process.

Checking the delivery

  1. Compare the delivery note with what is on the vehicle: producer, cultivar and count.
  2. Inspect the load: are bins overfilled, damaged or dirty? Is fruit exposed to sun, or wet?
  3. Look for obvious problems: rot, bruising, foreign objects (stones, glass, plastic), or a mix of cultivars.
  4. Check pulp temperature of sample fruit if the procedure requires it.
  5. Take samples for QC tests as instructed (maturity, defects).

Report problems to the intake supervisor. A delivery may be accepted, accepted with notes, held for QC decision, or rejected according to the packhouse rules. Never accept fruit without the required documentation.

lessons.title: Handling, placing and recording received fruit
lessons.html:
Offloading

  • Bins are offloaded by trained forklift drivers. Keep people clear of the vehicle and forklift path.
  • Handle bins gently. Dropping a full bin bruises fruit throughout.
  • Do not stack bins higher than the safe limit, and check that bins are stable.

Where fruit goes

Depending on the plan, received fruit goes to:

DestinationWhen
Drench or pre-treatment areaIf bins are drenched before storage, as per the treatment programme
Pre-cooling or bin cold storeIf fruit will be packed later; field heat must be removed quickly
Directly to the packing lineIf scheduled for immediate packing
Hold areaIf waiting for a QC decision

Fruit must never stand in the sun waiting for space. If the intake area is full, inform the supervisor so the plan can be adjusted.

Recording and stock

  • Enter the intake on the stock system or intake register immediately.
  • Record where the bins are placed (room and position).
  • Keep bins from different producers, orchards and cultivars separate.
  • File delivery notes and QC results with the intake number.

Bin and crate control

Bins are expensive and are usually returned to farms. Record bins received and empty bins returned. Damaged bins should be removed from use because they can injure fruit and people. Empty bins must be cleaned before going back to the orchard if required by the hygiene programme.

Hygiene and safety

  • Keep the intake area clean of fallen fruit, leaves and mud.
  • Do not allow animals or unauthorised vehicles in the area.
  • Wear high-visibility clothing and safety shoes; make eye contact with forklift and truck drivers.
  • Report vehicles leaking oil or fuel.

Communication

Tell the packing manager about the volumes and quality received, so that packing can be planned. Inform producers of problems such as high decay or foreign objects so they can correct them.

Key points

  • Intake is the start of traceability; capture producer, orchard, cultivar, bins and date.
  • Check the delivery against the note and inspect the load.
  • Take QC samples and report problems for a decision.
  • Move fruit quickly to treatment, cooling, packing or hold; never leave it in the sun.
  • Keep batches separate and record bin movements.
